name: Tomas Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Whatever you say is confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven at the Eastvale Power depot, by the ring road. Most of my work is underground distribution on the new housing estates, so digging trenches, laying ducts, pulling cable through them and helping the jointers. Some days we're on the older overhead lines in the suburbs, and I'm the one on the ground passing things up. I'm an apprentice at 58, so I'm slow, but I'm strong, and I don't complain about mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a butcher. I had my own shop on the high street for 25 years, Rahman's, and when the second supermarket opened with its own meat counter, the shop was finished inside three years. I sold it at 55, kept the flat above it, and rent that out now. My brother-in-law works at Eastvale and said they were short of people, and the pay was good, so here I am. I like that the power doesn't care what supermarkets do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, then. At the depot I'd say it to Josh, the lad I sit with at break, who's always reading about robots on his phone. I'm not online much, maybe the family group chat, and I'd just say good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I carry on. I do my apprenticeship, I get my card, I work till 65 and I retire with the rent from the flat and what I got for the shop. That's the plan, and nothing in this picture touches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas keeps going exactly as he is, turning up at seven and learning the trade. He'd keep using the work-order app only because the depot insists on it, and keep the money from the shop sale in the bank where it's been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather forecast that says no storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you only use the app because they insist. How does that go day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, our foreman, has given up asking me to use it on site. I write the job on paper and then put it in the app at the end of the day, which takes me twenty minutes when Josh would take two. She calls it my homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the supermarket story shape how you see AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Everyone told me the supermarkets wouldn't bother with proper meat, and then they did. So I don't believe anyone who says it's all hype, and I don't believe anyone who says it'll change everything. I wait and see what actually comes through the door.

S0.say: I'd just say well, that's that, then. I'd tell Josh at the depot and say good in the family group chat, since I'm hardly online.
S0.think: Privately he carries on with his plan: finish the apprenticeship, work till 65, and retire on the flat's rent and the shop money. Nothing in this picture touches that.
S0.do: Keeps going as he is, starting at seven and learning the trade. Uses the work-order app only because the depot insists and leaves the shop money where it's been.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast with no storm in it.
S0.quote: Bev, our foreman, has given up asking me to use it on site.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas speaks plainly and in short bursts. Losing his butcher's shop to supermarkets left him distrustful of both hype and doom, so he waits for what actually arrives. He avoids technology even when it costs him time, writing jobs on paper first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it will be good and some will be rubbish, like everything. At the depot I'd say I'll learn it if I have to. I wouldn't say much more than that, because people get worked up over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I'd let on. I'm already the slow one with the app. If the job turns into screens and sensors, I'm the one who looks useless, and I've been the one standing in an empty shop before. I don't want that feeling again at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would wait to see what Eastvale actually brings in before doing anything, and keep his head down at work. He'd stop dipping into his savings for small things, like the new garden shed he'd planned, and put the shed money aside instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about money, about being made to feel old and slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through a big change before with the shop. What did you do then that you'd do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I waited too long. I kept thinking customers would come back, and I spent two years of savings keeping the lights on. This time I'd still wait a bit, but I'd set myself a date, and if it's going badly by then, I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your wife Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, we've got the flat and the money. Then I'd probably go quiet for a week. She knows that's how I think things through.

S1.say: I'd say some of it will be good and some rubbish, like everything, and that I'll learn it if I have to. I wouldn't say more, because people get worked up over nothing.
S1.think: Privately it worries him more than he'd admit, because he's already the slow one with technology. He has stood in an empty shop before and doesn't want to feel useless again at 60.
S1.do: Waits to see what Eastvale actually brings in and keeps his head down at work. Puts aside the money he'd planned for a new garden shed instead of spending it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, not about money but about being made to feel old and slow.
S1.quote: I've been the one standing in an empty shop before.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between his public shrug and his private fear of being made obsolete a second time. He's learned from the shop that waiting too long cost him savings, so he'd set a deadline this time. His money is secure, but the emotional memory of losing his shop is strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and the companies should have seen it coming, both of them. At the depot I'd say there's no point getting angry, we can't stop it. I'd probably say it louder in the family chat, because that's where I argue with my son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the shop all over again but faster. I'd be 60, nowhere near my card, and the robots would be pulling cable before I'd learned to joint it. Money's not the problem. Being pushed out of a second thing I chose, that's the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would retire at 60 instead of 65, as soon as it was clear the robots were coming to Eastvale. He'd cancel the camper van he and Nadia have been looking at and keep that money as a cushion. He'd live on the flat's rent and the shop money until his pension starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit bitter. I'd be telling everyone I'm fine and lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very little warning. What does that short time change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't even pretend there's time to learn. With two years I wouldn't bother fighting it, I'd just get out with my dignity before they ask me to. I did the fighting with the shop and it only cost me money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money's not the problem, but you'd cancel the camper van. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both are true. We'd be all right, but I'd want to see where the prices go and whether tenants can still pay rent on the flat. You don't buy a camper van when you don't know if your tenant still has a job.

S2.say: I'd say the government and the companies should both have seen it coming. At the depot I'd say there's no point getting angry, and I'd argue louder in the family chat with my son.
S2.think: Privately it feels like losing the shop again, only faster, at 60 and nowhere near his card. Money isn't the issue; being pushed out of a second career he chose is.
S2.do: Retires at 60 instead of 65 once robots are clearly coming to Eastvale. Cancels the planned camper van to keep that money as a cushion and lives on the flat's rent and the shop money until his pension.
S2.feel: Anxious and a little bitter, saying he's fine while doing sums at night.
S2.quote: You don't buy a camper van when you don't know if your tenant still has a job.
S2.fieldNote: Tomas blames both government and companies evenly, which fits his centre outlook. With two years, he'd leave rather than fight, because fighting for his shop only cost him money. The camper van contradiction shows how a secure person still braces when the wider economy wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to make a plan. At the depot I'd say let's see what Eastvale says. I'd want the company and the council to tell us straight what's happening to the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is roughly what I need. I'd get my card in two years, work a few more, and be 63 when it arrives. Then I'd stop a couple of years early, which I can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas would keep going with his apprenticeship and get his card, keep putting a bit aside each month from the flat's rent, and plan to retire at 63. He'd tell Bev early that he's not interested in any robot training, so it goes to a younger worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's manageable. There's time to finish properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why turn down the robot training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not the right man for it, and Josh is. It would be wasted on me. I'd rather someone with thirty years ahead of them gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those five years at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably sort the flat out so it's easy to rent for a long time, new boiler, new windows. If things get strange, I want a flat that a tenant doesn't want to leave. That's the butcher in me, look after what you've got.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time for sensible people to make a plan. I'd want the company and the council to tell us straight what's happening to the jobs.
S3.think: Privately five years is roughly what he needs to get his card and work a few more years. He'd be 63 when it arrives and could stop a couple of years early.
S3.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship, earns his card and saves a bit from the flat's rent each month. Plans to retire at 63 and tells his foreman early to give any robot training to a younger worker.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, with time to finish properly.
S3.quote: That's the butcher in me, look after what you've got.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Tomas finish on his own terms, which matters more to him than the money. He'd step aside from robot training so a younger colleague benefits, a quiet generosity. His instinct with change is to look after what he owns, like the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody can complain they weren't told. At the depot I'd say let's not worry about 2036 in 2026. I'd leave the online stuff to Josh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm retired by then. I'd be 65 in 2033 and stop, three years before it arrives. Whatever robots pull cable on the estates in 2036, it won't be my business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas keeps going with his plan unchanged: apprenticeship, card, work until 65. He'd keep the flat rented and the shop money in the bank, and wouldn't learn anything new he didn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years feel compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm pushed out. Ten years, I walk out on my own feet. That's the whole difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Sami. He's an accountant, and Josh tells me the computers will do his job before mine. I'd tell him to have a plan, but he never listens to me, so I'd tell Nadia to tell him.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody can say they weren't told. At the depot I'd say there's no sense worrying about 2036 in 2026.
S4.think: Privately he'd be retired by then, stopping at 65 in 2033. Whatever robots pull cable on the estates in 2036 won't be his concern.
S4.do: Keeps going with his plan unchanged: apprenticeship, card and work until 65. Keeps the flat rented and the shop money in the bank, avoiding new skills he doesn't need.
S4.feel: Calm, as if it's someone else's storm.
S4.quote: Ten years, I walk out on my own feet.
S4.fieldNote: The amount of warning time maps directly onto Tomas's dignity: two years means being pushed, ten means leaving on his own terms. His worry moves to his son's accounting job. He'd pass advice through his wife, a small family detail that rings true.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be pushed out of my second job the way I was pushed out of the shop, before I'd finished anything. What would help is plain talk from Eastvale and the government about what's coming, and a fair way for older ones like me to leave early without losing our pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. When I had the shop, people came in for a chat as much as for sausages. On the estates now, people bring us tea when we're digging outside their house. A robot doesn't get the tea, and I think people will miss that more than they know.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't get the tea, and I think people will miss that more than they know.
portrait: Tomas Rahman owned a butcher's shop for 25 years until a supermarket finished it, then sold up at 55 and joined Eastvale Power as an apprentice cable layer. He's plain-spoken, avoids technology, and writes jobs on paper before typing them in. He has plenty of money from the shop and a rented flat, so his fear is about being made to feel old and pushed out a second time. In the fast AGI picture he'd retire at 60 and cancel the camper van, while the slower pictures let him finish his card and leave on his own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be pushed out of his second job before finishing anything, as he was with the shop.
whatWouldHelp: Plain talk from the company and government about what's coming, and a fair way for older workers to leave early without losing their pension.
